utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I was informed that the Prosecution had a preliminary issue to raise, and that it took so little time that we already could ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. As little as that, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wanted to follow up on Exhibit P6946 from yesterday, it was the decision forbidding the return of Croats and Muslims from the Ilidza War Commission. According to the document, it was dated 4 April 1993. Yesterday at transcript page 28860 the Chamber asked if the parties had any further information that would shed light on the date because at the end of the session there was some confusion about whether it was 1992 or 1993. The Prosecution would note that Exhibit P4906 is the decisions establishing the war commissions, it is dated 10 June 1992. The Prosecution also verified that the second session of the Ilidza War Commission was held on 27 February 1993. Based on this information, it appears clear that P6946 reflects the correct dates in April 1993. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the position of the Prosecution. If the Defence has anything to add, then we would like to hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do not dispute this date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. 1993. The date on that document is the actual date. Good morning, Mr. Mandic. Before you give evidence the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to make that declaration, of which the text is handed out to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the usher to provide the witness with a clean copy of his statement, it's with him, it's checked by the Prosecution. So I just want to inform the Chamber then that the witness has his clean statement in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, would you be so kind to tell us for the record your full name?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Bosko Mandic. Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough. I will occasionally make a pause; it doesn't mean that you should go on speaking, I'm just waiting for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have on our screens 1D1630, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mandic, have you given a statement to the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement before you on the screen and in the hard copy?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see the signature, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 2 of the statement. I need paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you drew my attention to the date written here. Which date should it be?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: It should be 30 April 1992, 30th April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After this correction, are the facts stated in this statement accurate as you told them to the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is the content of the statement accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put to you the same questions today, would you answer the same?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I believe so, maybe not 100 per cent but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Overall it would be?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, overall it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this statement into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1630 receives number D826.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D826 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honours, I would read statement summary of this witness. It's not that short, but I will not have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Mandic started to work for the Prijedor Municipal Assembly on 16th April 1992 when he was appointed vice chairman of the Executive Committee. After Slovenia and Croatia had seceded from the SFRY and as the national parties of the HDZ and SDA were established, the Serbian people realised that they had to get politically organised so as not to experience the suffering they had been through during World War II. As the result of these efforts, on 9 January 1992 the Assembly of the Republika Srpska was formed and the Serbian Assembly of Prijedor was established as well. On 29th April 1992, the police in Prijedor intercepted the telegram from Alija Delimustafic and Jerko Doko, the ministers of the interior and defence of the B&H, ordering an attack against the Serbs and the JNA. This pushed Serbs to take over the power in Prijedor on the next day, 30th of April, 1992. Following a peaceful take-over of power in Prijedor, the Council for National Defence decided to set up a Crisis Staff for municipality of Prijedor. Mr. Mandic was a member of this Crisis Staff. After this take-over of power SDS continued to negotiate with the SDA representatives. There were no armed conflicts after this take-over until Muslim forces attacked military conscripts in Hambarine on 22nd of May and military convoy in Kozarac two days later. On the 30th of May, 1992, Muslim forces attacked town of Prijedor. This resulted in war operations on the whole territory of the Prijedor municipality. At the same time a war broke out across B&H territory. The situation in Prijedor municipality was affected by the large number of Serbs -- Serb refugees coming from the towns that had already been taken in the Muslim-controlled areas in Bihac, Krupa, Sarajevo, Zenica, Tuzla, as well as from Croatia. The situation was very tense. At the same time Prijedor area had been cut off from Serbia and Montenegro and eastern parts of Republika Srpska. All those non-Serbs who did not violate the law, did not possess weapons, and decided to leave Prijedor town were helped by the local authorities during this process. This departure was made possible and organised through the Red Cross in Prijedor and International Red Cross. All the persons who took part in combat and had illegal weapons and military equipment had to be interviewed and investigated. At some point the decision was taken to organise this in Omarska because of the facilities it afforded. Curfew was introduced for all citizens. The telephone lines of all the citizens of Prijedor were disconnected. At the same time, there was a shortage of electricity in the entire Republika Srpska, including the municipality of Prijedor. Following the take-over of power, as the name suggests, the Muslim and Croat cadres in the Prijedor Municipal Assembly lost power. All the others kept their jobs. The problem was that some of the Muslims and Croats refused to support Republika Srpska which was only in the making, were not loyal to it either, and did not report for work. After the lapse of a specific number of days, they had to be dismissed under the pain of law and replaced by the others in order for the service in question to continue operating. And this was the statement summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Mandic, just to -- these were -- you have no further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do not have further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, just for your understanding that doesn't mean that there's no further evidence before since no further questions are put to you. The evidence you have given is in the statement which is now admitted into evidence, and you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Tieger or Mr. -- Mr. Tieger. You'll find Mr. Tieger to your right. Mr. Tieger is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, if I can have the interpretation a bit louder, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The usher will assist you in increasing the volume. Does this help?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let's begin with the last point covered in the summary by Mr. Lukic. In paragraph 41 of your statement you assert that "stepping down," that is, removal from positions following the take-over of power by Serb authorities, "had to do with respect for the constitution and law and not with ethnicity." Mr. Mandic, the reality is that there were, in fact, explicit decisions that were grounded on ethnicity, providing that only personnel of Serbian ethnicity could hold executive and other posts; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: How shall I put it? It's partly correct, and I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can explain it in the context of a document that, in fact, reflects such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could call up 65 ter 3304, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As we can see on the screen in front of you, this is a document dated the 22nd of June, 1992, reflecting a decision by the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, that: "Only personnel of Serbian ethnicity may hold executive posts, posts where the information flow is possible and the protection of socially owned property, that is, all posts of importance for the functioning of economic entities."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 3 of the English, please, and page 2 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We see a document from the very next day, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not have the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a document dated the very next day, the 23rd of June, 1992, signed by Milomir Stakic, the president of the Prijedor Crisis Staff, forwarding the decision we just looked at for implementation. Now, that's the reality of the situation at the time, isn't it, Mr. Mandic, unreflected in your statement to this Court?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, to whom was this sent?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, you were on the Crisis Staff at the time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The chronology, as you can clearly see it, is that the ARK Crisis Staff made a decision on the 22nd of June, grounded on ethnicity; it was received by Prijedor within 24 hours; the Prijedor Crisis Staff, of which you were a member, made a decision that they should forward that decision of the ARK Crisis Staff, that ethnically based decision for termination, so that it would be implemented. Isn't that the reality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we can see the first page, and I think it would be only fair to read the third paragraph from point 1 to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can do so -- if there's anything I'll have a look at it. And, Mr. Tieger, if there's unfairness in it, you'll certainly be aware of it, otherwise the matter can be dealt with in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Still, I would like to have the first page in front of the witness so he can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you are not examining the witness at this moment, Mr. Lukic. But I'll have a look at it, and you are drawing my attention to the first page and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Point 1, paragraph 3, under the point 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Point 1, paragraph 3. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was going to cover that, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- and it specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed then and we'll wait. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you've had a chance to see the ARK Crisis Staff decision, you've had a chance to see the Prijedor Crisis Staff decision, forwarding that for implementation. That's a reflection of the fact that terminations were based on ethnicity and not, as you say in your statement, not based on ethnicity at all but on respect for the constitution. Isn't that the reality of the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: We know that the Serbian Democratic Party took over power. It's logical that it appointed and removed senior personnel. Where somebody would be appointed, the SDS would decide. Where employees didn't show up for work, decisions were made to dismiss them and other people were appointed in their place. I think that's only logical. There were employees who were not disturbed in any way because they continued to be loyal to the existing laws. They accepted things and of course -- for instance, we had a business with 500 employees called GIK Mrakovica where Mr. Ibro, a man of Muslim faith, continued to be the manager. But it would be logical for the public security station or the army to replace staff and make new appointments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: -- and of course -- I just want to emphasise one more thing, if you allow me. We did not enforce this decision blindly. There were senior staff who were not Serbs but continued in their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, that was an elaborate explanation of the "logic" that you claim underpinned termination decisions. But this decision or these two decisions don't describe that at all. They have a categorical provision based on ethnicity and that decision was made by the ARK Crisis Staff, received by the Prijedor Crisis Staff, and sent for implementation by the Prijedor Crisis Staff. That is true, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to this paper. But on the ground it wasn't like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender 3304, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 3304 receives number P6948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic was interested in the third paragraph of provision 1. You emphasise in your statement that only the issue of respect for constitution as a bench-mark for terminations, but the reality, Mr. Mandic, as reflected in the ARK Crisis Staff decision was that it was loyalty and fidelity to the party that was the bench-mark for terminations, not loyalty to the constitution. And isn't that what the first provision in this decision reflects? That's the last paragraph of the first part of that decision. It's about loyalty to the party, isn't it, and the decision that posts cannot be held by people who haven't accepted that the SDS is the only representative for the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: That pertained to Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we understand that non-Serbs who were loyal to the SDA [sic] would be excluded from this provision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand that question. It's somehow complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not complicated. You've just told us that the last paragraph of provision 1 relates to the Serbs only, and I'm saying -- and you have just told us also that there was a man who headed a company who was a non-Serb because he was loyal. Now I'm saying: Does this last paragraph exclude non-Serbs who are loyal to the SDA -- SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There weren't any such persons in the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you've told us of a person who retained his job as a manager of a company who was non-Serb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And didn't he -- and why was he retained in his job when everybody else who was non-Serb was dismissed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he was loyal to the then-authorities. He was not a member of the party. He did not exhibit any extreme tensions and of course thereby he remained in that position. That was the reason. Had there been anything, he certainly would have been prosecuted. He kept his job, he supported the then-government, so why would he not stay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the then-government and the then-authority was the SDS government, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So he was loyal to the SDS and its government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he wasn't a member of the SDS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not saying --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but he was loyal to the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not saying he was a member, I'm saying he's loyal. You have just told us. He was loyal [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the government, to the authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. You said everybody who was loyal to the then-authorities would be covered by this, but he must be Serb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, I did not look at his birth certificate. You can tell who is who on the basis of a name, but you cannot really go in-depth that much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have told this Chamber that that person was a non-Serb. Whether or not you had looked at his birth certificate, you know him to be a non-Serb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you are not able to answer my question? My question, if I must remind you: Does this paragraph, the last paragraph of provision 1, not include non-Serbs, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you -- this is not the first time you've testified before a Chamber in this institution. You testified in the Karadzic case as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in your testimony in the Karadzic case, you referred to the fact that as vice chairman of the Executive Board you did not travel to Banja Luka unlike other Prijedor officials; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was the responsibility, as you testified, of the president of the municipality and other Prijedor representatives to go to Banja Luka for meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the Prijedor authorities implemented the decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff, as we have already seen from the document we've previously examined; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you another example of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could call up 65 ter 17422, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 22nd of May, 1992, sent by the Prijedor Crisis Staff to all commercial and social enterprises, in accordance, as the document states, with the decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, imposing permanent operational duty in all the municipalities of the ARK, and that's an example of Prijedor's implementation of the decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff as you mentioned a moment ago; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours 17422 receives number P6949.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, in paragraph 6 of your statement you refer to the "peaceful" take-over of power in Prijedor, what you have corrected to be the 30th of April, 1992. Now, I want to clarify first that when, although you say "peaceful," that means nothing more than no bloodshed. It does not mean no force. It was a forcible take-over; correct? That is, the Serbs occupied buildings with armed personnel -- physically occupied those buildings?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: That was done by the police, milicija, that is to say the public security station. They took over these facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 9 you state that that take-over was the result of intercepted telegrams that caused "panic" among police and citizens. Now, in actual fact, Mr. Mandic, the take-over of Prijedor by the Bosnian Serb authorities was planned and preparatory actions were being put in place well before those telegrams; isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: First of all, I mean, I am not a Bosnian Serb. I'm a Serb from Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm offended as a person if somebody says "Bosnian Serb" or "Bosnian" to me. I'm a Serb from Bosnia-Herzegovina and my religion is Orthodox Christianity. I'm sorry for this reaction, but I really had to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When and where were you addressed as a Bosnian Serb being a witness here? I saw that -- I heard Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- talking at the Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He didn't address you in any way in person. So would you please answer the question rather than complain about the language used which was not directly related to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. That was my understanding and that is why I reacted. I apologise if it wasn't addressed to me. As for a response to this question, it was logical that as the SDA and the HDZ were preparing to take over Bosnia and Herzegovina, the SDS worked on the ground, and of course they talked to these two parties all the time as well so that the problem of Prijedor and Bosnia-Herzegovina could be resolved by peaceful means. We offered all sorts of options, even a joint police force including Serbs and non-Serbs, mixed patrols and so on. However, when this telegram arrived then a decision was made to take-over authority in Prijedor in a non-violent way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, your statement indicates that the cause and effect of the Prijedor was, A, the telegram that was intercepted or the two telegrams that were intercepted; and thereafter a reaction, an immediate reaction, a panicky reaction by the police. There is no mention whatsoever of any preparatory steps or any prior decision to implement the take-over in Prijedor. Now, first of all, are you acknowledging to this Court now that there were -- that there was a prior decision, that is, before those telegrams were sent and intercepted to take over-power, and that steps were taken to implement that decision before the receipt of those telegrams, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you admitted that when you were testifying in the Karadzic case. I'm going to turn you to that testimony now, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn to 65 ter 31659, page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were asked about this same issue because you raised it in your Karadzic statement as well, and you were confronted with the fact - and I can read you all this verbatim but let's see first if my description of what happened in the Karadzic case jogs your recollection. You were first confronted with a fact at page 9 in the e-court that the Serb authorities had been preparing the take-over long before the 29th of April. You provided a fairly elaborate answer similar to the one you did today: "We were aware of the time that we lived in. We were aware of the history ... we knew that the representatives of the SDA ... had decided to take over the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina ...," you referred to World War II. Then you were asked: "Well, then, do you agree ... that the SDS was preparing the take-over ... long before receiving the Telex?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And again, you said: Well, we had to organise ourselves in one way or another. You were then confronted with a Prijedor SJB report, which was P2968 in the Karadzic case, as reflected here, and is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For the benefit of counsel and Your Honours, P3948 in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- a document which reflects that activities were launched to prepare for a take-over by force. These activities gained momentum in April. It refers to the "very detailed preparations" and talks about the role of 400 policemen in carrying out the take-over. And then you were asked: "Now as this police report makes clear, this take-over by the SDS in Prijedor was planned long before the Telex was received on the 29th of April; correct?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's at the bottom of page 10 in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at the top of page 11 in e-court, you say: "Yes. But this was not the only reason. I mean, the Cazin Krajina." So in the Karadzic case you acknowledged that the take-over by the SDS in Prijedor was planned long before the Telex was received; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, it's very questionable what that means, a lot earlier, long before, it could be a month or more or five years or whatever. When --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the Municipal Assembly could not have been established --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You're asking questions yourself rather than answering them, but tell us how long before was it that it was prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think it was from the beginning of April when a member of a Serb wedding party was killed in Sarajevo, that that became intensified then, and what was discussed was what would happen if something like that would happen in Prijedor. But it was the telegram that initiated this. I apologise. And everything else I said when I testified in the case of President Karadzic, those reasons are also the ones that led to the take-over on the 30th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it -- you said there were more reasons. The issue raised by Mr. Tieger simply is, in paragraph 9 of your statement you give a picture that a telegram triggered everything, whereas - as you tell us now - a month before you were already thinking about how to prepare, et cetera. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the testimony provided in Mr. Karadzic's case shows that I confirmed that, so here in my statement it is abbreviated, it's two sentences only. I did not say why and on account of what, et cetera. The telegram was the one that led to this happening in the municipality of Prijedor, so there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's not the whole truth? It's part of the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, nobody asked me to describe what had happened earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You gave a picture as if it was all triggered by the telegram. You're now telling us that events before played a role as well and you testified in a similar way in the Karadzic case, so you must have been aware that that is relevant information, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, and I confirmed that on the basis of conversations. I didn't hide anything. This is what led to the decision for the take-over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We leave it to that, and I remind you that you are supposed to tell the whole truth and not just part of it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. So I don't run afoul of the Court's schedule, is it -- okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Similarly, Mr. Mandic, in paragraph 6 you state that the Crisis Staff was established or set up after the take-over. And that's not true either, is it? The Crisis Staff existed in Prijedor before the take-over, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we have P3779, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, only my colleague would be specific, which Crisis Staff he asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are more Crisis Staffs --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then, Mr. Lukic, you took a statement, then I take it that you would have created clarity in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was describing the Crisis Staff this gentleman was a member of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is -- I don't want to interfere with the questions, only there are more Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then the question to the witness: Was there a Crisis Staff, perhaps another one, created before the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if I can just intervene slightly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't consider that to be a precisely fair intervention. The question was clear I was asking about the Prijedor Crisis Staff. Now that intervention is clearly an interpretive queue for the witness. It's not -- it doesn't clarify an ambiguous question. The question is about whether or not the Prijedor Crisis Staff existed. The witness is in a position to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, Mr. Lukic, the Crisis Staff the witness is talking about in paragraph 6. He was taken to paragraph 6 and the question is put to him whether the Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which refers to the Crisis Staff he is talking about in paragraph 6 to set up a Crisis Staff in order to more easily overcome. Witness, was the Crisis Staff you're talking about in paragraph 6 established after the take-over or was it established at any earlier point in time? You are -- you're reading from the screen. As a matter of fact, we'd like to hear your answer first rather than to read from the screen. Was the Crisis Staff you are talking about in paragraph 6 established before the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, I mean the Crisis Staff of the Serb municipality of Prijedor, it was established after the 30th of April, that is to say on the basis of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, Mr. Lukic, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have documents on this. It's not in dispute I think at all. I can tell you the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I had a whole case on the Crisis Staff in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's about reliability and credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly, that's why I'm trying to have a fair question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was fair. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you, Mr. Mandic, is P3779, a document dated the 23rd of April, 1992, among other things it refers in point 5 to "... working on the take-over, co-ordination with the JNA notwithstanding." And in points 2 and 3 it refers to the fact that: "All units and staff in management posts shall be responsible and subordinate to the Crisis Staff in this area." And point 3: "To reinforce the Crisis Staff according to speciality." Now, that's a reflection of the existence of the Crisis Staff on at least April 23rd, 1992, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I really don't know when this Crisis Staff was established. I mean, in 1991 I didn't live in Prijedor, in Bosnia-Herzegovina at all. This is certainly organisation on the ground by the SDS; that is to say, Crisis Staffs were established and local committees because the other sides did that too in order, I mean, to get information on the ground. Well, that would be it, my answer, because -- well, the Crisis Staff -- perhaps the person who wrote this was taking notes. I don't remember officially a Crisis Staff as an institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But you attended this meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But I really don't know if there was a Crisis Staff when it was established. As for what I know, I know that the Serb municipality of Prijedor was established on the 9th of January, but then a Crisis Staff and who was on this Crisis Staff and who was the main person there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to be getting into that in some greater detail in a moment, but since we're just a couple of minutes from the break, perhaps it's better to pick it up fresh when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take the break now and, Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, in connection with the establishment of the Crisis Staff and the take-over, I wanted to call up a number of documents that shed light on both of those issues. And the first one I'd like to call up is P3038, a document the Court will be familiar with. Mr. Mandic, these are the instructions for the organisation and operation of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in emergency conditions, dated the 19th of December, 1991, often referred to as the Variant A and B document. It provides for measures and tasks in connection with municipalities where the Serbian people constitute a majority, that's Variant A; and in those municipalities where the Serbian people do not constitute a majority, that is Variant B. And it's broken down into different into two different levels or phases or steps, level 1 and level 2. So, first of all, let me ask you if you claim to be familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: May I answer? In 1991 I was not in Bosnia-Herzegovina at all. In fact, it was the former Yugoslavia still and I never held this document in my hands. I never read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. We're going to track this document and Prijedor in a moment, but first let me ask you to confirm a very basic proposition in connection with issue of Serb majority or Serb minority municipalities. It's correct that in 1991 Prijedor had about 112.500 people, of whom a little over 49.000 were Muslims and -- well, 49.350 were Muslims and 47.580 were Serbs with smaller groups of -- smaller other groups; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I think it was correct under the census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could I seek clarification of one of the previous answers. You said you never held this document in your hands, you never read it. You never read it in your whole life or did you intend to say that you didn't read it in 1991 or early 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not active at that time in the sense of receiving any documentation and in 1991 I was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that was not my question, whether you were active or not. My simple question is whether you ever in your life read this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. I can't answer this question. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put another question to the witness? You said: "In 1991 I was not in Bosnia-Herzegovina at all. In fact, it was the former Yugoslavia still..." When did you return to the former Yugoslavia or Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that was just before the new year, 1992, the 24th or 25th December. I was working in Germany and there are witnesses who can testify where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In your statement, paragraph 3, you say: "I stayed in Germany for about a year and returned to Prijedor in late 1991." I just want to clarify what is late 1991, you are saying now 24th or 25th December.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could call up P3773, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, what you'll see coming up on the screen next, Mr. Mandic, is a document about eight days later from the 27th of December, 1991, a meeting of the Prijedor Municipal Boards, and as we look down the page we can see that President Miskovic, the president of the SDS Municipal Board, read out the instructions forwarded to the Prijedor SDS by the Assembly of the Serbian People, referred to the two versions but noted that only version II, which in context I take to be version -- Variant B which was relevant for Prijedor was read out. And then having read them out, he explained what had been done so far with respect to the instructions. And as we look further down the page we see the reference to the reasons and functions being stated for the establishment of the municipal Crisis Staff and local staffs on the territory of the municipality. Turning the page in English but remaining on the same page in B/C/S, we see the decision to introduce around-the-clock duty in SDS offices. We note in point 2 that the composition of the Crisis Staff is identified. And finally that a session of the Assembly of the Serbian people was scheduled. Now, Mr. Mandic, either at that time or at some point later when you took a more active part in the organs of the Serbian people in Prijedor, were you made aware of the fact that the Prijedor Serbian authorities, the SDS, had received the Variant A and B instructions and was implementing them, including by establishing a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I joined in later and I remember individual people advocated various things. For instance, late Mirko Sarac was in charge of economic affairs and I talked to him mostly about the economy. At any rate, there were some people but I really didn't know who was in charge of what exactly and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it's true the Crisis Staff was established at that time but I didn't immediately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. After a few lines you come to an answer to the question. Why not do that directly? But it's only the second part of the question. Had you become aware then that the Prijedor Serbian authorities, the SDS, had received the Variant A and B instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certainly I was not aware of it, but it's obvious that it's a fact. The document speaks to it. There's no reason for me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there's only one reason for you: That is, to answer the question. You say you were not aware, then the simple answer is: No, I was not aware. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this Chamber has received evidence that on the 14th of February, 1992, Dr. Karadzic at a large extended meeting of the Executive and Main Boards and municipality presidents and so on activated the second level of Variant A and B, referring to it four times and concluding by -- let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this is P3774.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Concluding by saying: "That's why we called you today, to intensify, to introduce the second level and to intensify the functioning of the government at any cost and on every single millimetre of our territory." That was not so long before you say you became vice-president of the Executive Committee. Were you made aware of the fact that the second level of Variant A and B had been activated by the president of the SDS in mid-February?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: If I was at some meeting, this must have been shown to me; I mean, a meeting of the Municipal Board of the SDS. Now, whether I remember what Radovan Karadzic said or not, I'm not sure, but I was informed if I attended that meeting. If there is a document about it, I accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me turn in that case to 65 ter 15948.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can kindly ask that the English translation be released in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As we can now all see, Mr. Mandic, this is a document dated the 17th of February, 1992, three days after the activation of level 2 by Dr. Karadzic. It's a meeting of the SDS Prijedor Municipal Board. And the first speaker was Mr. Miskovic, the president of the SDS Municipal Board, who gave a briefing on the meeting held in Sarajevo, and describes it beginning with his description that Mr. Karadzic was the main speaker. And if we look further down the page and turn to page -- and you'll see it, sir, on page 2 of the B/C/S, about six lines -- six, seven lines down, Mr. Miskovic informs the attendees as he's debriefing them on the meeting that in view of all that he's described and all that Dr. Karadzic explained, "it is necessary to activate the second stage of the position stated by the SDS BH Main Board ..." And he goes on to explain what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that would be reflected on page 3 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English. That is not the correct page 2. I'm not sure what that reflects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. There, it's about six lines down where

utterances.speaker: MR. MISKOVIC EXPLAINS
utterances.text: "It is necessary for us to establish control in our territories."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Mandic, if we turn to the next page in English and I believe page 4 in the B/C/S but we'll look at both pages, you'll see your name mentioned in between Mr. Coric's intervention and Mr. Drljaca's comments, you'll see the name "Mandic." So, Mr. Mandic, does this refresh your recollection about being present at a meeting when Prijedor's -- when the discussion about the activation of the second level of Variant A and B was made known to the relevant Prijedor authorities and the implementation discussed?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present, indubitably, and the transcript confirms it. But to tell you the truth what A and B means -- I mean, plan A is a bit lighter -- I mean, I would have to read it. It was such a long time ago. I need to see what's written in that plan B, but it involves certainly organisation, monitoring on the terrain, on the ground, some kind of preparation because it's obvious we knew that the war was coming, it never spared us and it wasn't going to spare us that time and it's not going to spare us the next time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Mandic, Mr. Mandic, Mr. Mandic, I don't think it is necessary for you -- it's not necessary to read the document. I think what Mr. Tieger is -- the point he's making is that you attended this meeting before the 30th of April, 1992, where the establishment of a Crisis Staff is being discussed. So if -- do you agree with him on that? Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree, if that's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document with 65 ter number 15948 receives number P6950.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you mentioned a moment ago that you would be interested in looking at portions of the Variant A and B document. Let me turn your attention then to a few pertinent portions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if we can call back P3038.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as Mr. Miskovic did on December 27th, I'll turn my attention to Variant B, the relevant part of this document as far as Prijedor is concerned, that begins on page 6. And at page 7 of the English and also page 7 of the B/C/S, we see references at points 5 to "carrying out preparations for the establishment of municipal government organs (the Executive Committee, administration organs ...," et cetera. And reference to "preparing the take-over of the staff and some of the equipment of security services centres and their integration with the public security station ..." And then turning to the second level on page 9 of the English and pages 8 and 9 of the B/C/S, we see the following. The first provides for: "Convene a session of the Serbian Municipal Assembly and establish a municipal Executive Committee, establish municipal government organs ...," et cetera. "2. Mobilise all Serbian police forces and gradually resubordinate them in co-ordination with JNA commands and staffs." "4. Organise round the clock physical security and of all public buildings of vital interest, transport, and communications," et cetera. Now, those provisions I just read out to you, Mr. Mandic, describe the take-over; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Not at that moment, but on the 30th of April -- I mean, you can't just take over power by coming there without having personnel ready who will sit there giving them instructions how to act --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you carefully listen to the question. Mr. Tieger did not put to you that at that point in time the take-over was a fact, but he says that what is described here as the second level in effect is a description of a take-over, whether you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, I agree. I understood it differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And to press a bit further, that's what happened in Prijedor and the take-over in Prijedor on April 30th, as I believe you just alluded to, was pursuant to the second level of Variant A and B; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct, that's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could call 65 ter 31663, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, again, the answer "that's written here." What is written there, did that -- was that performed, executed on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Perhaps you could move slightly back from the microphone, so as to avoid any further interference. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I've just called up the abridged minutes of the 5th Session of the Serbian municipality of Prijedor held on the 16th of April, 1992. It reflects the nomination of Executive Committee members and so on, as we see on the first page. And as we see on the second page, we see the election of the following people, including yourself. So there's you, Mr. Mandic, as the Executive Committee deputy chairman; Mr. Budimir, the National Defence secretary; Mr. Drljaca, the chief of the SJB; Mr. Kuruzovic, the TO staff commander, and so on among the many offices planned. And again, these reflect steps taken shortly before and in anticipation of the take-over to come; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 31663 receives number P6951.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could have 65 ter 10845, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this is a dispatch from Simo Drljaca to the Banja Luka CSB dated the 30th of April, 1992. He notes that: "In accordance with the conclusions of the Executive Board, the ... control was seized over the SJBs and all other major facilities ..." And he also refers to the fact that ten police stations and 1.587 policemen were mobilised." Now, the mobilisation of the policemen is a reflection - and I can refer you back to the document, but since we've referred specifically to it just moments earlier - a reflection of the second -- but point 2 of this second level of the Variant B in the Variant A and B document, correct? And that's what Mr. Drljaca is referring to and that's what was executed by him. Sorry, I just wanted you to confirm that the reference --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he acted upon this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 10845 receives number P6952.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let me turn to a different aspect of your statement. In paragraphs 43 through 44 you emphasise that there was no contact with the authorities in Pale for "several months after the war started." Now, I take it that means from the beginning of April 1992 until sometime in the summer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask the following: I had this question -- this kind of question put to me during the case of President Karadzic, and I really could not recall the time, was it April, May, June. But then we reached the following: Information was received from Pale in the AR Krajina, but the time of the attack on Prijedor and the breakthrough of the corridor, I mean that period remained without any functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's break it down and let's focus on -- first on what you remember right now and what you're in a position to tell this Chamber right now. So first of all, let's start with the easy part: And that is when the break in communication that you claim began, when you claim it began. And I take it from your statement you're referring to the beginning of the war and the nature of the problems, that means the beginning of April 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: No, I'm referring to the time in Prijedor. I wasn't looking at all of Bosnia-Herzegovina here in my answer. When there was no electricity, when communications were down because of war operations in the Prijedor municipality, that's the period I mean that we had no communication, otherwise we had normal communication. I think up until the 15th of May, 20th of May, and then I think there was no communication until the corridor was established, and I'm referring to Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when was the corridor established in your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 28th of June, 1992. I was there so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're talking about a period earliest 15th of May, latest 28th of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not several months, that's one month and a half, isn't it, at its best?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, when I was writing I wasn't paying attention but that's it. I mean, I wasn't paying attention to this, what a month or two meant. I mean, I'm not a lawyer so quite simply I write -- well, it wasn't my wish to do anything wrong in any sense. It just so happened that -- well, two months, a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that I made a mistake, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You attested to it after having read it again, if I understand you well, and it's not the first time now that you are correcting yourself. And please keep this in mind that we expect accurate --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- accurate testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can talk about some of those contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we call up 65 ter 31043, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: These, Mr. Mandic, are the minutes of the Prijedor Municipal Board from the 18th of May, 1992. And on the agenda in point 2 we see report from the session of the Serbian republic Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly, and that report was given by Simo Miskovic, as we see in item 2, noting that: "There were 18 items on the agenda, the main guide-lines in future activities were identified, the commander of the Army Supreme Staff appointed, members of the Presidency of the Republic elected, et cetera." Now, that would be a reference to the 16th Assembly Session of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina held in Banja Luka on the 12th of May, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Sorry, is that written here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger referred to the date of the Assembly session which is discussed at this meeting, the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I just don't know the date. I can't see the date. Maybe it was then, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Mandic, the date is not that significant for this purpose. All right. Now, the reference that we saw before, that is, Miskovic briefing the members of this meeting, including yourself, about the main guide-lines in future activities, that was a reference to the strategic objectives of the Bosnian Serbs or the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina which were articulated by Dr. Karadzic at that Assembly session in Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document with number 31043 receives number P6953.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And after that assembly session and after the meeting that we just looked at, Prijedor authorities were implementing [Realtime transcript read in error "admitting"] the decisions of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that would include the following document --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could call up P3417.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you do that, Mr. Tieger, page 37, line 16, did you say implementing or admitting?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After this session -- the sentence reads: "After the session and after the meeting that we just looked at --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. -- implementing, correct. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You were calling?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was P3417.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a decision taken at the meeting held on the 22nd of May, 1992, about the mobilisation on the territory of the Prijedor municipality. As we see on the second page of the English but on the single page in B/C/S, it was signed by Dr. Stakic. And in the preamble we see that it was pursuant to the decision of the Serbian republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina about the general mobilisation of forces and materiel in the republic. So this is an example of the Prijedor Crisis Staff and Prijedor Serbian authorities implementing the decisions of the republic-level authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, I want now to turn to portions of your statement dealing with particular events in Prijedor, and specifically events having to do with Hambarine and Kozarac. In your statement, as you will recall, you refer to the attack on Hambarine on about the 22nd of May or 23rd of May, 1992. And in your statement you refer to the fact that a number of Muslims left Hambarine around the time of the attack. Mr. Mandic, it's correct, isn't it, that the reason Muslims from Hambarine might have been inclined to leave prior to the commencement of the attack is because the Crisis Staff threatened them that their safety was in jeopardy if the ultimatum of the Crisis Staff to hand over the alleged perpetrators of the check-point incident was not fulfilled. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, partly. I mean, really what the Crisis Staff, I mean, over Radio Prijedor broadcast to the public, well, yes, that's the decision. But the non-Serb and Serb population moved out before the take-over and that could be seen from my statement. Women, children, and the elderly did not wait for the month of May to see what would happen then. They left a lot earlier. Of course when there is a lack of safety people do flee, and the Serb population facing the belt where Hambarine is also sought shelter from the war operations. They didn't stay at home. That's only natural. No one knew who would win ultimately and it's logical for people to withdraw if the extremists do not hand over those who killed the soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You state here that the non-Serb and Serb population moved out before the take-over. That seems to be all-embracing. Of course that's not true, right? You're suggesting that some people moved out, but you know very well that most people remained, many of whom - many of whom - ended up in detention facilities in Prijedor after the attacks began.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Many people moved out of Prijedor before the take-over. I lived in town and I knew through Sun Tours buses left every day. At first we wondered why, and then later on we realised why. I'm not saying that everybody left, but a lot of people left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the issue apparently is: Did most of the people leave or did most of the people stay? So some -- let's talk about did the majority stay or did the majority of non-Serbs leave Hambarine before the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stayed, the majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The majority stayed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you also claim at paragraph 11 that there was "strong resistance to the police and army action at Hambarine." In fact, Mr. Mandic, the VRS didn't suffer any casualties at all; right? And you acknowledged that in your testimony in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, those were the reports that we received. It's not that I knew -- I mean, I read in Kozarski Vjesnik that one soldier had been wounded. So the report said that there was strong resistance. I wasn't there but that is what was presented in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So according to you the report said that there was strong resistance resulting in the wounding of one soldier and the destruction of the -- virtually the entire community of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: That is what the report says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also testified that the -- or you provided in your statement that the purpose of the operation was to remove the check-point and bring those allegedly responsible for the check-point incident to justice, that's the last line of paragraph 10 of your statement. In fact, the army's --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- the army's response to this check-point incident was to shell the entire village; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that that is natural in war operations. If somebody fires at the army, what else can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was not whether it's natural or whether it's justified. The question simply was whether the army's response to this check-point incident was to shell the entire village, and I take it from your answer that you say yes that's what happened, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then shortly thereafter, Mr. Mandic, the same thing happened to Kozarac, right? There was a two- or three-day shelling, intensive shelling of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And again in your statement you referred to -- and in connection with that you were also aware, were you not, that hundreds of people, that is Muslims, were killed in these operations?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know. I did not take part in these operations. I wasn't counting how many people were there, who was there. If there's a report that this was submitted to the Crisis Staff, then it is logical that I should accept that I was made aware of that. Now, how many, I mean really that was not my line of work, to deal with the number of people who had been taken prisoner and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Speaking of your line of work, sir, you referred in your Karadzic testimony to the fact that you did not follow what the army and the police were doing. That was their own line of work. So I take it that -- first of all, you recall that testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer. The interpreters could not hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, yes, because through the Crisis Staff I was made aware of all of these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. But they had their own chains of command and you were not privy to their individual communications, right, internally?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't communicate also. When Prijedor was taken over during the first days -- can I say this? Mr. Miskovic -- no, sorry, Drljaca refused co-operation. He got up and left the session because I asked him where the golden money were going, the golden money they took away from the people. Quite simply, I wanted to know and I didn't want us to have a bad reputation that we were looting, that we were robbing people; however, he didn't like that. He got up and left the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So in light of what you've just explained about your line of work and the chain -- unitary chains of command of the army and the police, when you say in paragraph 33 of your statement: "The army and the police did not have permission or orders to contravene international laws of war or the Geneva Conventions." You're not in a position to know if that's true or not, are you, according to you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I was not checking of them exactly. Everybody knew about the Geneva Convention and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, I want to turn next to some of your evidence about the camps. First of all, the Municipal Assembly and the offices where you and other Prijedor political officials functioned were located in and around the centre of town; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that would be a relatively short distance, maybe a kilometre or so from Keraterm; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, sort of, 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In paragraph 17 of your statement, you assert that the Trnopolje camp was established for the civilian population which did not want to participate in the conflict with the Serbs. Now, first of all, by that you meant the Muslim and Croat by "civilian population"; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: These camps, Trnopolje, Keraterm, and Omarska, were established at the end of May; correct? That is, May 1992.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And shortly after that, by the beginning of June, 1992, as many as 7.000 or more Muslims and Croats were detained in those three facilities; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Maybe I cannot remember the exact figure, I mean how many. Believe me, I don't know the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were aware that there were thousands, however; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, thousands. Not 1-, 2-, but maybe 3-, 4-, 5- as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, we can break now. I anticipate concluding well before the estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you give me -- we'll take a break in a second. Do I understand that you agree that people were detained at Trnopolje camp and Keraterm and Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First I have to provide an explanation. Omarska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- one cannot equate Omarska, Trnopolje, and Keraterm. These are different things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Were people detained in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That -- because you're -- a minute ago you said that people were detained there, including Trnopolje. We'll take a break first. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. We resume at ten minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, before we'll continue, one short question. Have you ever visited Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean during the war operations? At the time of war operations I never went there. I went there either in the end of August or early September together with the president of the municipality. We went around the schoolhouse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you have no personal knowledge about what happened there before you went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I mean, I have some knowledge from what people were saying, but I was never in Omarska or Keraterm or Trnopolje myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say "September," September of which year were you there at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn to P3891, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a summary of conclusions adopted by the Prijedor municipality Executive Committee relating to police matters between April 29th and 17th August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we turn to the third page in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The third item from the bottom provides, refers to: "Conclusion number 01-023-45/92 of 2 July 1992, forbidding the individual release of persons from Trnopolje, Omarska, and Keraterm." It's clear from this conclusion, Mr. Mandic, that people in Trnopolje were detained there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember I think the reasons were mainly preventative. Those people left the compound during the day and returned for the night. It was possible that some mines were left over on the ground, that there would be drunken soldiers going around. It was for their own protection. I believe this conclusion was made for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So people in Trnopolje, Omarska, and Keraterm, according to you, were detained but detained for their own good; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: That's how it was in Trnopolje. In the other two camps they were investigation centres. A triage was done after the attack on Prijedor and Kozarac. There were people carrying weapons. And this part of the work was handled by the police, I believe there are records of these interviews. When I'm talking about safety reasons, protecting the population, I'm talking about Trnopolje. As for Omarska and Keraterm, I think there was no freedom of movement, apart from the transport of those from Keraterm who were not carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, with respect to Keraterm and Omarska, that's a reflection of what you said in paragraph 47 of your statement in which you claimed that the interviewing and investigation of persons who took part in combat and who had illegal weapons and military equipment was organised in Omarska. Now, first of all, before I continue on that, the organs that were interrogating people there were the military and police organs; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: There were inspectors, but exactly of what profile, from which branch, I don't know. I know that there were some inspectors from the active-duty complement and the reserve complement, but whether they were only from the police or only from the army or combined, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the truth is is that Omarska and Keraterm were full of non-Serbs who had nothing to do with combat or weapons; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: What can I accept or not if that's how it was? I don't know who was held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You have told this Court in your statement that people who participated in combat and had weapons were held in Omarska and interrogated. So your position is now that you don't know that and it could very well be the case that the people held in Omarska and Keraterm were civilians who had nothing to do with combat or weaponry; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Possibly. I even heard that some Serbs were there, not only non-Serbs. There were Serbs also in Omarska. How they got to be there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, it happened now several times that you're telling us that what is found in your statement that you just don't know, and that's not what we expect from a witness. We expect a witness to tell us what he knows for certain. You say you don't know who was detained in Omarska, whereas in your statement you give a totally different impression.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I had no insight myself, but I would hear things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- you know, I never got to see any lists or physically see these people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
